subChunks.title: Biochemistry — Metabolism, Enzymes & Proteins

storyBeats.txt: Theodora held up a glucose molecule model. "This one sugar," she said, "contains about 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁸ joules of chemical energy. When it is oxidised completely by your cells, that energy becomes ATP — the currency your body uses to do everything from contracting a muscle to synthesising a protein to generating a nerve impulse. Life is thermodynamics. It is chemistry. And the chemistry is extraordinarily elegant."

"Enzymes are the reason life is possible at room temperature. The spontaneous combustion of glucose in air occurs at several hundred degrees Celsius. Enzymes allow cells to extract the same energy at 37°C — by providing a reaction pathway with a far lower activation energy. Every metabolic transformation in your body is catalysed by an enzyme, and each enzyme was itself built according to the instructions encoded in a gene."

"Proteins are the molecular machines of life — not just enzymes, but structural components, transporters, receptors, hormones, antibodies, and motors. Their function is entirely determined by their three-dimensional shape, which is entirely determined by their amino acid sequence, which is entirely determined by the DNA code. From sequence to structure to function: the central paradigm of molecular biology."

subChunks.hookHtml: Biochemistry studies the chemical processes within living organisms — particularly the structure, function, and interactions of biomolecules: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Metabolism encompasses all chemical reactions that occur in a cell, organised into anabolic pathways (building up complex molecules, requiring energy) and catabolic pathways (breaking down complex molecules, releasing energy). Understanding biochemistry is the molecular foundation of medicine, nutrition, pharmacology, and biotechnology.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Biomolecules

Carbohydrates: Composed of C, H, O in approximate ratio CH₂O. Functions: energy (glucose), energy storage (glycogen in animals, starch in plants), structural (cellulose in plant cell walls, chitin in insect exoskeletons). Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose) → disaccharides (sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose = glucose + galactose) → polysaccharides.

Lipids: Fats and oils (triglycerides — glycerol + 3 fatty acids), phospholipids (glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate group — form cell membranes; amphipathic), steroids (cholesterol — membrane fluidity, steroid hormone precursor), waxes, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Saturated fatty acids: no C=C double bonds, solid at room temperature. Unsaturated: one or more C=C bonds (cis configuration in natural unsaturated fats → kinked chains, liquid at room temperature). Trans fats: artificially produced unsaturated fats with trans configuration — associated with cardiovascular disease.

Proteins: Polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds (−CO−NH−). 20 standard amino acids, each with the same backbone but different R-groups (side chains) that determine properties (polar, non-polar, charged, aromatic). Protein structure: Primary (sequence of amino acids), Secondary (alpha-helix and beta-sheet formed by hydrogen bonds between backbone groups), Tertiary (3D folding determined by R-group interactions — hydrophobic core, disulfide bonds, ionic interactions, H-bonds), Quaternary (multiple polypeptide chains — e.g. haemoglobin: 4 subunits).

Nucleic acids: DNA and RNA — polymers of nucleotides (base + sugar + phosphate). Covered in genetics modules.

Enzymes

Enzymes are biological catalysts — proteins (and some RNA molecules = ribozymes) that accelerate reactions by lowering activation energy. They are not consumed in reactions and are highly specific (one enzyme, typically one reaction or closely related group).

Active site: The region of the enzyme where substrate binds and the reaction occurs. Complementary shape/chemistry to the substrate.

Lock-and-key model: Substrate fits the active site precisely — rigid complementarity. Induced fit model (more accurate): active site changes shape slightly on substrate binding to optimise fit — explains why some related substrates are also acted on.

Enzyme kinetics (Michaelis-Menten): Rate = V_max[S]/(K_m + [S]). At low [S]: rate ≈ V_max[S]/K_m (first order). At high [S]: rate → V_max (zero order — enzyme saturated). K_m = substrate concentration at half V_max — measures enzyme-substrate affinity (low K_m = high affinity).

Enzyme inhibition:

  • Competitive inhibition: Inhibitor resembles substrate, binds active site, competes with substrate. Effect overcome by high [S]. Increases apparent K_m; V_max unchanged.
  • Non-competitive inhibition: Inhibitor binds elsewhere (allosteric site), changing active site shape. Not overcome by high [S]. V_max reduced; K_m unchanged.
  • Irreversible inhibition: Inhibitor covalently binds active site — permanently inactivates enzyme. Example: aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX enzymes; organophosphate nerve agents irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase.

Factors affecting enzyme activity: Temperature (rate increases with T until optimum ≈37°C for human enzymes; above optimum, denaturation occurs as H-bonds break, active site distorted). pH (enzymes have an optimal pH; extremes disrupt ionic interactions and H-bonds — pepsin optimum pH ≈2 [stomach acid], salivary amylase optimum pH ≈7 [mouth]).

Metabolism — Cellular Respiration

Aerobic respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ≈30–32 ATP. Three stages:

Glycolysis (cytoplasm, no O₂ needed): Glucose (6C) → 2 pyruvate (3C). Net yield: 2 ATP, 2 NADH. Substrate-level phosphorylation.

Krebs cycle / Citric acid cycle (mitochondrial matrix): Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (2C) + CO₂. Acetyl-CoA enters cycle → 2CO₂ released per turn, producing NADH, FADH₂, and 1 ATP per turn. 2 turns per glucose. Primary function: generate electron carriers (NADH, FADH₂).

Electron transport chain (ETC) / Oxidative phosphorylation (inner mitochondrial membrane): NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to protein complexes → electrons pass along chain → O₂ is the final electron acceptor (reduced to H₂O) → proton (H⁺) gradient across inner membrane → H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase → ≈26–28 ATP produced. This is chemiosmosis (Mitchell, Nobel Prize 1978).

Anaerobic respiration: Without O₂: glycolysis generates 2 ATP but pyruvate cannot enter Krebs cycle. In animals: pyruvate → lactic acid (regenerates NAD⁺ for glycolysis to continue — temporary, during intense exercise). In yeast: pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂ (alcoholic fermentation).

Photosynthesis

6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Two stages:

Light-dependent reactions (thylakoid membrane): Light energy absorbed by chlorophyll → excites electrons → electron transport → ATP and NADPH produced; H₂O split (photolysis) → O₂ released. Photosystems I and II.

Calvin cycle / Light-independent reactions (stroma): CO₂ fixed by RuBisCO enzyme → reduced using ATP and NADPH → G3P → glucose. For 1 glucose: 3 turns of cycle, consuming 9 ATP and 6 NADPH.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why a fever (high body temperature) can be dangerous, using your knowledge of enzyme structure and the effect of temperature on enzyme activity.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: An experiment investigates the effect of pH on catalase activity. Catalase is an enzyme found in liver cells that breaks down hydrogen peroxide: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. Liver discs are placed in buffer solutions of pH 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10. Hydrogen peroxide solution is added, and the volume of O₂ gas produced in 60 seconds is measured. Results: pH 4: 2 mL; pH 5: 8 mL; pH 6: 18 mL; pH 7: 32 mL; pH 8: 28 mL; pH 9: 15 mL; pH 10: 3 mL. (1) Plot these results (describe what the graph would look like). (2) Identify the optimum pH and explain why catalase has this optimum. (3) Explain why activity is reduced at pH 4 and pH 10. (4) A student adds a competitive inhibitor at pH 7. Describe the effect on the rate and how it could be distinguished from non-competitive inhibition experimentally. (5) Identify TWO variables that must be controlled in this experiment.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Graph: a bell-shaped curve with pH on the x-axis (4–10) and volume of O₂ on the y-axis (0–32+ mL). The curve rises from pH 4, reaches a peak at pH 7, then falls symmetrically (though pH 8 is slightly closer to optimum than pH 6, so the curve is slightly right-skewed). The graph shows a clear optimum at pH 7 with reduced activity at both extremes.

(2) Optimum pH = 7. Catalase (found in cytoplasm and peroxisomes, pH ≈7) has evolved an active site with a precise 3D shape maintained by ionic interactions, hydrogen bonds, and hydrophobic interactions between amino acid R-groups. At pH 7, these interactions are optimal, active site geometry is correct, and the substrate (H₂O₂) binds with maximum affinity. This represents the physiological pH of the intracellular environment where catalase normally functions.

(3) Reduced activity at pH extremes: At pH 4 and pH 10, H⁺ or OH⁻ ion concentrations are far from the optimum. Extreme pH disrupts the ionic interactions and hydrogen bonds between charged amino acid R-groups (e.g. -NH₃⁺ and -COO⁻ groups). This causes conformational change — the tertiary structure of the enzyme is altered → active site shape changes → substrate cannot bind as effectively (or at all). At very extreme pH, denaturation is irreversible — the enzyme unfolds completely and loses function permanently. The ionic state of catalytic residues in the active site also changes (protonation/deprotonation), disrupting catalysis directly.

(4) Competitive inhibitor effect at pH 7: reduces rate (volume of O₂ produced in 60 s) because the inhibitor occupies some active sites, reducing the number available to H₂O₂. However, increasing [H₂O₂] concentration would overcome competitive inhibition — at sufficiently high substrate concentration, the inhibitor is outcompeted, and V_max is restored. To distinguish: Non-competitive inhibitor: increasing [H₂O₂] does NOT restore the rate to original V_max — V_max is permanently reduced because the inhibitor binds a different site, changing active site shape regardless of substrate concentration. Experimental test: vary [H₂O₂] at constant inhibitor concentration and compare rates with and without inhibitor. If V_max is restored at high [S]: competitive. If V_max is reduced regardless: non-competitive.

(5) Controlled variables must include: (a) Temperature — all reactions at the same temperature (e.g. 25°C in a water bath); temperature affects both enzyme activity and gas solubility. (b) Concentration of H₂O₂ — same volume and concentration of substrate added in each test; different [H₂O₂] would alter rate independently of pH. Other valid variables: surface area of liver discs (same size), volume/mass of liver tissue, time allowed (60 s in all conditions), same equipment/collection method for O₂.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: During intense exercise, muscle cells switch from aerobic to anaerobic respiration. (1) Explain why this switch occurs — what is happening to the oxygen supply, and what is the immediate biochemical problem for the muscle cell? (2) Describe the anaerobic pathway in human muscle — what happens to pyruvate, and what is the purpose of this reaction? (3) Lactic acid (lactate) accumulates during intense exercise, causing the burning sensation in muscles. Explain why continued accumulation of lactate eventually stops the muscle from contracting. (4) After exercise stops, the body enters the 'oxygen debt' (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, EPOC) phase. Explain what the extra oxygen is being used for. (5) Marathon runners preferentially use aerobic respiration throughout, while sprinters rely heavily on anaerobic. Explain the physiological reason for this difference and the metabolic consequences for recovery after each type of event.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Switch to anaerobic: during intense exercise, cardiac output and respiratory rate cannot increase fast enough to deliver O₂ to muscle cells at the rate they are consuming it — the demand for ATP exceeds the aerobic supply rate. Without sufficient O₂ as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain (ETC), the ETC stalls → NADH cannot be re-oxidised to NAD⁺ → glycolysis runs out of NAD⁺ (since glycolysis produces NADH and requires NAD⁺ to continue). Without NAD⁺, glycolysis stops → ATP production from glycolysis also stops. The immediate biochemical problem: regenerating NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue to produce ATP.

(2) Anaerobic pathway in muscle (lactic acid fermentation): Pyruvate (from glycolysis) is reduced by NADH → lactate (lactic acid) + NAD⁺. The enzyme is lactate dehydrogenase. Purpose: the reduction of pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD⁺, which allows glycolysis to continue operating and producing 2 ATP per glucose anaerobically. Lactate itself is not merely a waste product — it is transported to the liver (Cori cycle) where it is converted back to glucose (gluconeogenesis), replenishing blood glucose. Anaerobic yield: only 2 ATP per glucose (vs 30–32 aerobically) — extremely inefficient, which is why it cannot be sustained indefinitely.

(3) Lactate accumulation and muscle fatigue: the lactate-producing reaction also releases H⁺ (lactic acid dissociates: CH₃CHOHCOOH → CH₃CHOHCOO⁻ + H⁺). Rising H⁺ concentration → intracellular pH falls (acidosis, from ≈7.1 to ≈6.6 during intense exercise). Low pH: (a) directly inhibits contractile proteins (troponin and myosin ATPase are pH-sensitive — reduced Ca²⁺ sensitivity); (b) inhibits phosphofructokinase (PFK), a key glycolytic enzyme → slowing ATP production further; (c) reduces Ca²⁺ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum → weaker muscle contraction. These combined effects cause muscle fatigue and force the athlete to reduce exercise intensity below the anaerobic threshold.

(4) Oxygen debt (EPOC): after exercise, O₂ consumption remains elevated above resting for minutes to hours. Uses: (a) Reconvert lactate to glucose: liver uses O₂ via aerobic metabolism to drive gluconeogenesis (converting accumulated lactate back to glucose via Cori cycle). (b) Restore phosphocreatine (PCr) stores: PCr is a rapid ATP buffer (PCr + ADP → Cr + ATP, creatine kinase) depleted during exercise; rephosphorylation requires oxidative phosphorylation. (c) Restore O₂ stores: myoglobin (muscle O₂ store) and haemoglobin in blood need to be re-oxygenated. (d) Elevated body temperature and metabolism: the body continues to metabolise at elevated rate as temperature returns to baseline — requiring additional O₂. (e) Protein repair and synthesis: damaged muscle fibres are repaired post-exercise.

(5) Marathon vs sprint metabolism: Marathon runners depend on aerobic respiration because: the aerobic pathway produces ≈15× more ATP per glucose and can also oxidise fatty acids (which provide even more ATP per gram than glucose but require O₂) — essential for sustaining effort over hours when glycogen stores are limited. Fat oxidation is virtually impossible anaerobically. Sprinters use anaerobic glycolysis because: maximum power output requires extremely rapid ATP production; anaerobic glycolysis produces ATP much faster per unit time than aerobic, even though it is less efficient overall. The ETC and Krebs cycle simply cannot cycle fast enough to meet maximal sprint demand. Metabolic consequences: Marathon recovery — glycogen repleted over 24–48 hours (carbohydrate loading), fatigue mainly from glycogen depletion and muscle damage accumulation ('hitting the wall' = glycogen exhaustion forcing reliance on fat → slower pace). Sprint recovery — primarily removing lactate (converted to glucose in liver over 30–60 min), restoring PCr (2–3 min), restoring O₂ stores (1–2 min). Sprinters recover much faster than marathon runners from individual efforts, but experience acute muscle damage from the intensity.
learningObjectives: Describe the four levels of protein structure and explain how tertiary structure determines enzyme function, including the active site and induced fit model.
Explain competitive and non-competitive enzyme inhibition, temperature and pH effects on enzyme activity, and Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
Trace the three stages of aerobic respiration (glycolysis, Krebs cycle, ETC) identifying the location, substrates, products, and ATP yield of each.
Explain why muscle cells switch to anaerobic respiration during intense exercise and describe the consequences for pH, muscle function, and recovery.
commonMistakes: Thinking enzymes are permanently destroyed by high temperature — at moderate temperatures above optimum, denaturation is reversible (cool the enzyme, it may refold); at very high temperatures, denaturation becomes irreversible; describing it as simply 'slowing down' above the optimum is incomplete.

Saying the Krebs cycle directly produces most of the ATP from respiration — the Krebs cycle mainly produces NADH and FADH₂ (electron carriers), which drive the electron transport chain to produce the majority of ATP; the Krebs cycle itself directly produces only 2 ATP per glucose.

Confusing competitive and non-competitive inhibition by effect — both reduce reaction rate, but only competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing [S]; non-competitive inhibition reduces V_max regardless of substrate concentration.

Treating lactic acid as the cause of the delayed muscle soreness after exercise (DOMS) — lactic acid is cleared within 30–60 minutes post-exercise; delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS, 24–72 hours later) is caused by microscopic muscle fibre damage and inflammatory response, not residual lactate.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly describes primary through quaternary protein structure with examples, and explains the relationship between tertiary structure and enzyme active site function.
Applies Michaelis-Menten kinetics correctly (K_m, V_max, [S] effects) and distinguishes competitive from non-competitive inhibition with experimental evidence.
Accurately traces the three stages of aerobic respiration with correct locations, products (NADH, FADH₂, ATP), and explains chemiosmosis.
Explains anaerobic respiration in muscle cells with the correct pathway, purpose (NAD⁺ regeneration), and physiological consequences (pH drop, muscle fatigue).

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Protein folding from a linear amino acid chain to a functional 3D structure is thermodynamically driven but requires assistance in vivo. Molecular chaperones (HSP70, GroEL) prevent misfolding and aggregation by binding unfolded or partially folded proteins and providing a sequestered environment for correct folding. Protein misfolding causes diseases: Alzheimer's (amyloid beta and tau aggregates), Parkinson's (alpha-synuclein), prion diseases (misfolded PrP). Understanding folding is a major goal of computational biology — AlphaFold2 (DeepMind, 2020) achieved near-experimental accuracy for predicting protein structures from sequence.

Many enzymes are regulated by molecules that bind at sites distant from the active site (allosteric sites), causing conformational changes that increase or decrease activity. Allosteric activators increase activity; inhibitors decrease it. Haemoglobin is the textbook allosteric protein: O₂ binding increases affinity for further O₂ binding (cooperativity — sigmoidal binding curve). ATP, AMP, and NADH act as allosteric regulators of multiple metabolic enzymes, coordinating glycolysis and the Krebs cycle to match ATP demand.

After a protein is synthesised, its function can be modified by chemical modifications to specific residues. Phosphorylation (serine, threonine, tyrosine residues — by kinases; reversed by phosphatases): turns enzymes on or off — central to cell signalling cascades. Glycosylation: adds sugar chains — important for cell-cell recognition, membrane targeting, immune function. Ubiquitination: flags proteins for degradation by the proteasome. PTMs dramatically expand the functional diversity of the proteome beyond what the genome alone encodes.

The large-scale study of all small molecules (metabolites) in a biological system — glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, nucleotides, cofactors. Metabolomics gives a snapshot of cellular metabolism at a moment in time. Techniques include NMR spectroscopy and mass spectrometry. Used to identify biomarkers for disease (metabolic profiles differ between healthy and diseased states), understand drug mechanisms, and optimise fermentation processes in industry. Complements genomics (genes), transcriptomics (mRNA), and proteomics (proteins) in systems biology.

rabbitHoleTerms.term: The Warburg Effect and Cancer Metabolism
rabbitHoleTerms.description: Otto Warburg (Nobel Prize 1931) observed that cancer cells preferentially use aerobic glycolysis (glycolysis even in the presence of O₂ — 'aerobic glycolysis' or 'Warburg effect') rather than oxidative phosphorylation, despite its inefficiency. This produces lactate even when O₂ is available. Proposed reason: rapidly proliferating cells need precursors (amino acids, fatty acids, nucleotides) for biosynthesis — glycolytic intermediates provide these; generating energy is secondary. The Warburg effect is the basis of PET scans (cancer cells take up ¹⁸F-glucose avidly — lit up on the scan). Understanding cancer metabolism is a major area of drug development.

questions.questionHtml: At which stage of aerobic respiration is the majority of ATP produced, and where in the cell does it occur?
options: Glycolysis — in the cytoplasm; produces ≈30 ATP per glucose
Krebs cycle — in the mitochondrial matrix; produces most ATP per turn
Oxidative phosphorylation / Electron transport chain — at the inner mitochondrial membrane; produces ≈26–28 ATP per glucose by chemiosmosis
The conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA — in the mitochondrial matrix; produces the most ATP
questions.correctAnswer: Oxidative phosphorylation / Electron transport chain — at the inner mitochondrial membrane; produces ≈26–28 ATP per glucose by chemiosmosis
questions.explanationHtml: ATP yield per glucose: Glycolysis: net 2 ATP. Pyruvate decarboxylation: 0 ATP directly. Krebs cycle: 2 ATP (1 per turn × 2 turns). Oxidative phosphorylation (ETC): ≈26–28 ATP (from 10 NADH + 2 FADH₂ produced in earlier stages; each NADH yields ≈2.5 ATP, each FADH₂ ≈1.5 ATP via the proton gradient). Total: ≈30–32 ATP per glucose. The ETC operates on the inner mitochondrial membrane — the electron carriers pass electrons through protein complexes (I, III, IV) → protons pumped across the membrane → H⁺ gradient → protons flow back through ATP synthase (Complex V) → drives rotation → phosphorylates ADP → ATP. This is chemiosmosis, described by Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis.

questions.questionHtml: A student adds increasing concentrations of substrate to an enzyme at constant enzyme concentration. Initially, rate increases proportionally with [S]. At high [S], the rate plateaus. The student then adds a non-competitive inhibitor at the highest [S] tested. What happens to the rate?
options: The rate increases because the high substrate concentration overcomes the inhibitor
The rate decreases — non-competitive inhibitors reduce V_max by binding an allosteric site and altering the active site, regardless of substrate concentration
The rate stays the same — at V_max, enzyme is already fully saturated and inhibitors cannot have an effect
The rate first increases then decreases — the inhibitor initially activates the enzyme then inhibits it
questions.correctAnswer: The rate decreases — non-competitive inhibitors reduce V_max by binding an allosteric site and altering the active site, regardless of substrate concentration
questions.explanationHtml: At high [S], the enzyme is already operating near V_max (all active sites are occupied by substrate most of the time). Adding a competitive inhibitor at this point would have little effect (substrate outcompetes it). But a non-competitive inhibitor binds the allosteric site — a different site from the active site. This changes the enzyme's conformation, distorting the active site geometry so that each enzyme-substrate interaction is less productive. The allosteric site is not blocked by substrate — both substrate and non-competitive inhibitor can bind simultaneously. Therefore, even when all active sites are occupied by substrate (high [S] → near V_max), the non-competitive inhibitor reduces the catalytic efficiency per enzyme-substrate complex → V_max is reduced. Rate decreases. The K_m (apparent affinity for substrate) is unchanged — the enzyme still binds substrate with the same affinity — but the maximum rate achievable with any amount of substrate is lower.

questions.questionHtml: Cyanide (CN⁻) inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) in the electron transport chain, blocking electron transfer to O₂. A student predicts: 'Cyanide should cause cells to produce more lactic acid.' Is this prediction correct, and why?
options: Incorrect — cyanide blocks the ETC but cells will simply switch to aerobic glycolysis to compensate without producing lactic acid

Correct — blocking Complex IV halts the ETC → NADH cannot be re-oxidised → NAD⁺ depleted → aerobic respiration stops → cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis → pyruvate reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺ → lactic acid accumulates
Incorrect — cyanide directly stimulates glycolysis, bypassing the ETC entirely without involving lactic acid
Correct — but only in muscle cells; other cell types do not produce lactic acid under any circumstances
questions.correctAnswer: Correct — blocking Complex IV halts the ETC → NADH cannot be re-oxidised → NAD⁺ depleted → aerobic respiration stops → cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis → pyruvate reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺ → lactic acid accumulates
questions.explanationHtml: The student's prediction is biochemically correct. The mechanism: (1) CN⁻ binds Fe³⁺ in cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), blocking electron transfer from cytochrome c to O₂. (2) Electrons back up along the ETC — Complexes I, II, III also stall → all electron carriers (ubiquinone, cytochromes) become fully reduced. (3) NADH cannot donate electrons to the stalled Complex I → NADH accumulates → NAD⁺ is depleted. (4) Glycolysis requires NAD⁺ (to continue producing ATP); the Krebs cycle also stalls. (5) To regenerate NAD⁺ and maintain some ATP production via glycolysis: pyruvate + NADH → lactate + NAD⁺ (lactate dehydrogenase). Lactic acid accumulates. Cyanide poisoning causes: rapid collapse of aerobic ATP production → energy failure → lactic acidosis (very high blood lactate) → metabolic acidosis → cellular dysfunction → death. Antidotes work by: (a) hydroxocobalamin (B12 derivative) — scavenges CN⁻; (b) sodium thiosulfate — provides sulfur for CN⁻ → SCN⁻ (thiocyanate, less toxic); (c) amyl nitrite → nitric oxide → methemoglobin → binds CN⁻ preferentially over cytochrome c.
